# jobs


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

Fetching a page, ingesting a batch of files or rebuilding the topic map
can fail or be interrupted.
[`Queue`](https://vedicreader.github.io/vishalakshi/jobs.html#queue)
keeps such work as rows in a `jobs` table in the vault’s own SQLite
file, so a job outlives the process that queued it, and no separate
server is needed. `enqueue` adds a job. A worker takes jobs with
`claim`, which marks them as running and gives the worker a lease: a
time limit (`lease`, 10 minutes) on its claim. Two workers claiming at
once never get the same job. If a worker dies, its lease runs out and
`reclaim` puts the job back. A job that fails is retried after a delay
that doubles each time, from 30 seconds up to 6 hours, and after
`max_attempts` (5) failures it becomes dead: it stays in the table, with
its error, for a person to look at.

Because the queue lives in the same file as the documents, a job queued
inside a `write_txn` is committed together with the write that caused
it. [`Queue`](https://vedicreader.github.io/vishalakshi/jobs.html#queue)
needs only a database and knows nothing about a vault;
[acquire](01_acquire.ipynb) registers the vault’s own jobs on it.

### backoff

``` python
def backoff(
    attempt:int, # failures so far; 1 on the first
    base:float=30, # first delay, seconds
    cap:float=21600, # longest delay, 6h
    jitter:float=0.25, # +/- fraction, so jobs that failed together do not retry together
)->float:
```

*The delay before the next attempt: `base` seconds doubled for each
failure so far, at most `cap`, with some random jitter.*

## The queue

A job has a `kind`, which names the handler that runs it, and a
`payload`, a dict stored as JSON. `key` makes queueing idempotent: while
a job with the same kind and key is still waiting or running, enqueueing
it again returns that job instead of adding a second one, so re-running
the same fan-out does not double the work. Lower `priority` runs first.

### Queue

``` python
def Queue(
    db, # open litesearch/fastlite Database; the queue lives in its file
    lease:float=600, # seconds a claim is held before another worker may take the job
    max_attempts:int=5, # attempts before a job is dead-lettered
    base:float=30, # first retry delay; doubles per attempt
    keep:float=604800, # how long finished jobs and run history survive `purge`, 7d
    busy_ms:int=30000, # lock wait before a write gives up; apsw's stock default is 100ms
):
```

*A job queue stored in an open litesearch database, which runs every job
at least once.*

### Claiming

`claim` picks and marks its jobs in a single SQL statement, and SQLite
lets only one write run at a time, so another worker cannot slip in
between the pick and the mark. What a worker gets back is already
running and already leased.

`ack` (finished) and `fail` (failed) only count while the caller still
holds the lease. A handler slower than `lease` has its job reclaimed and
given to another worker. Without this check its late `ack` could mark as
done a job another worker is still running, or its `fail` could send a
finished job back for a third run. Instead the late call comes back
`lost`, and the run history says so.

### Running

A handler is a function `fn(payload)`, registered with `register` or the
`on` decorator. `run_one` runs one claimed job, and `drain` claims and
runs until the queue is empty or `limit` jobs have run; it is what a
cron job calls. How a handler ends decides what happens next:

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>the handler</th>
<th>the job</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>returns normally</td>
<td>is done</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>returns a dict with <code>skipped</code></td>
<td>is done, recorded as a skip, and not retried; the acquisition
methods do this when a page has no transcript or is not a PDF</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>raises <a
href="https://vedicreader.github.io/vishalakshi/jobs.html#retry"><code>Retry</code></a></td>
<td>is retried after <code>Retry.after</code> seconds or the backoff
delay, using up an attempt; this is for work that did not fail but
should run again, such as a page behind a bot wall</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>raises any other exception</td>
<td>is retried after the backoff delay, and dead once its attempts are
spent</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>raises <a
href="https://vedicreader.github.io/vishalakshi/jobs.html#terminal"><code>Terminal</code></a></td>
<td>is dead at once</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

[`Terminal`](https://vedicreader.github.io/vishalakshi/jobs.html#terminal)
is for failures that waiting cannot fix: a 401, a model name that does
not exist, a file that is gone. With the default schedule a doomed job
would otherwise be retried for most of a day. A job whose kind has no
handler is dead at once for the same reason.

### Looking at it

`jobs` lists jobs by state and kind, `pending` counts what is left,
`stats` counts each state, and `history` lists past runs. Dead jobs are
the queue’s inbox for a person: `dead` lists them with the error that
finished them off, and since nothing is deleted on failure, `retry`
simply puts one back with its attempt count reset. `purge` deletes
finished jobs and run history older than `keep` (7 days) and leaves dead
jobs alone.

## Try it

``` python
from litesearch import database

db = database()
q  = Queue(db, lease=60, max_attempts=3, base=1)
seen = []
q.register('echo', lambda p: seen.append(p['n']) or dict(n=p['n']))
q.enqueue_all('echo', [dict(n=i) for i in range(3)])
q.drain('w1')
seen, q.stats()
```

    ([0, 1, 2], {'ready': 0, 'running': 0, 'done': 3, 'dead': 0, 'next_due': None})
